text: Domestic flies annoy poultry, pigs (especially farrowing/weaning pens), and cattle, and can spread or sustain disease, making population control important. Fly control means controlling larvae (maggots): eggs need about 35°C and high humidity to hatch, with manure being the ideal breeding site, along with waste feed, slurry crusts, wall cracks, and farrowing-house bedding — removing these breeding grounds breaks or reduces the reproductive cycle. Butox (2 ml/liter of water) is a low-environmental-toxicity insecticide usable both on animals and in resting areas — about 3–5 liters of solution treats a 250 kg animal, and 1 liter covers about 20 m² of wall. Horse flies bite painfully during the day and can cause real blood loss in numbers (20–30 flies can take about 20 teaspoons of blood every 6 hours); they are hard to control since they persist around animals, feed on poorly-sprayed areas like the underbelly and legs, and breed in hard-to-find wetland sites. Mosquitoes don't transmit disease to cattle directly, but heavy night-time biting disturbs rest, and since cattle are inactive/sleeping in daytime, this leads to poor grazing and declining condition; control (though not easy) comes from cutting grass, draining puddles, and removing all standing water, even small amounts.
